newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish budget to take winding path to statute book.
newsitem.headline: Danish budget to take winding path to statute book.

text.p: Failure to make a deal with opposition Conservatives leaves Denmark's minority government unable to ensure parliamentary support for its 1997 budget as a complete package and forced to pilot individual clauses through parliament, political sources said on Monday.

Negotiations between the Social-Democrat-led coalition and the Conservatives ground to a halt on Friday after intense overnight talks, with the right rejecting government plans to finance a balanced budget by increasing taxes.
"With the financing model that the government proposed, we were unable to give our agreement," Conservative Leader Hans Engell told reporters after the final meeting.
A Conservative official told Reuters on Monday that the party would not, however, vote against the budget in parliament.

A political source said that only in the most extreme circumstances would a mainstream parliamentary party attempt to stop a budget becoming law, but if the government wanted the extra security of an advance guarantee it had to pay for it.
"In this case the government was unable to make the concessions that the Conservatives saw as necessary to present to their voters as the justification for an accord," she said.
The way ahead is one used regularly by minority governments produced by Denmark's proportional electoral system.

The budget proposal will be split into a number of separate bills for the financing of health, education, welfare and other areas, each one with its natural supporters to the right or left of the centre-left government providing a majority.
Defence spending is not an issue this year as it was tied up in a four-year agreement as part of the 1996 deal.
An aide to Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft said on Monday that he had not yet decided how to separate the 1997 package or how to aim its components.

"He's walking around and thinking. My guess is that he will invite the different parties in parliament to some sort of talks during this week but I still don't know yet when or who," the aide told Reuters.
He added that the parliamentary Christmas recess, the deadline for getting the 1997 finance bill approved, begins this year on December 19. "So there's still plenty of time."
The largest opposition party, the Liberals, have been subdued throughout the horsetrading between the government and the Conservatives.
The two traditionally negotiated with the government as a team until the Conservatives surprised everybody by making a separate deal on the 1996 budget.
Liberal Deputy Chairman Anders Fogh Rasmussen said over the weekend that he hoped that the failure of this year's attempt would reunite the right-of-centre camp.
"It would be completely natural now for us to begin a joint effort with the Conservatives," he said.
The broad framework of the 1997 budget is already known.

Lykketoft has said that he plans to bring the public sector deficit into balance in 1997, from its 1996 deficit of 5.8 billion Danish crowns. The talks with the Conservatives foundered on where to make specific savings.

The government hopes to reduce the overall state budget deficit to 19.3 billion crowns from the 1996 shortfall of 28.5 billion, cutting 1997 state debt to 59.3 percent of Gross Domestic Product from 60 percent in 1996.
It attributes the shrinking deficit in part to lower unemloyment and higher tax and VAT revenues accruing from increased consumption.
The fall would bring debt within the limits for membership of European Economomic and Monetary Union although Denmark, one of a handful of countries fulfilling the criteria, has opted out in advance.
